title: Characterizing Longitudinal Gut Motility in Mice via Transit Time and Immunostaining
author: Frith, Kashyap, et al.

steps.title: Plan experimental timeline
steps.instruction: Create a detailed timeline for experimental manipulations, transit‑testing dates and endpoints (e.g., target day ± 5 days, measurements 2 days before and after). Conduct a pilot study to estimate sample size and define “red” pellet criteria.

steps.title: Prepare 6 % carmine dye
steps.instruction: Make 0.5 % methylcellulose, dissolve carmine powder, autoclave and vortex aliquots before use.

substeps.instruction: Heat 10 mL water to ≥ 80 °C in a glass beaker; add methylcellulose powder with light agitation; stir until particles disperse.
Add 20 mL cold water/ice to lower temperature; cool to 0–5 °C for 20–40 min; continue agitation ≥ 30 min after reaching temperature.
Weigh 1.8 g carmine powder (handle gently, non‑toxic) and add to cooled methylcellulose solution; agitate at 18–25 °C for ~30 min until evenly dispersed.
Autoclave the solution (liquid cycle) in a vessel ≥ 2.5 × the solution volume; do not tighten lid before autoclaving.
Vortex aliquots on the day of testing as dye may separate.

steps.title: Prepare fecal collection tubes (optional)
steps.instruction: Label two microcentrifuge tubes per animal; pre‑weigh one tube on an analytical balance and record the weight for later fecal water fraction or microbiome analysis.

steps.title: Define red pellet criteria
steps.instruction: Consider a pellet “red” only when it is fully saturated with dye (no specks or partial coloration).

steps.title: Set up transit‑testing cages
steps.instruction: Place one clean mouse cage on white paper inside a biosafety cabinet, insert a stainless‑steel raised‑floor cage insert, add a food/water hopper with lid, and have a water bottle ready (add 1–2 food pellets after mouse is placed).

substeps.instruction: Ensure the steel insert allows stool to fall through the grating, keeping pellets out of mouse reach.
Return mouse to home cage after the transit test.

steps.title: Prepare silicone plates for tissue harvest
steps.instruction: Mix Sylgard 184 base and curing agent per manufacturer, dispense into 6‑well plates, 12‑well plates, 24‑well plates, medium and large petri dishes to cover bottoms ≥ 0.5 cm depth (≈ 25 mL per 6‑well, ≈ 35 mL per 15 cm dish). Cure 4–5 days at 18–25 °C, then cover with lids.

steps.title: Gather tissue‑harvest supplies
steps.instruction: Collect ice bin with ice, dry‑ice foam box, glass dissection plate, silicone‑coated 6‑well plates, 4 large pipette tips, ruler, dissection tools, peristaltic pump with tubing, beaker, PBS, butterfly needle, Zamboni fixative, 4 % PFA in PBS, weigh boat with PBS, O.C.T., embedding molds, stainless‑steel pins, RNAlater or 40 % glycerol in PBS, carcass disposal bag, and foam box with dry ice.

substeps.instruction: Do NOT use anodized pins; use stainless‑steel pins only.

steps.title: Ensure equipment availability
steps.instruction: Confirm access to a dissection hood (for PFA or pathogen work) and any other required instruments.

steps.title: Label all containers and molds
steps.instruction: Label tubes, silicone plates, and embedding molds with animal ID, tissue type, and date (e.g., two RNAlater tubes for small and large intestine, one glycerol tube for cecum).

steps.title: Prime peristaltic pump
steps.instruction: Set pump flow rate to 3–5 mL/min and prime tubing with PBS before any transcardial perfusion.

steps.title: Prepare fixation and buffer solutions
steps.instruction: Prepare PBS with 40 % glycerol, phosphate‑buffered saline, Zamboni fixative, PBS with 10 % sucrose, and PBS with 20 % sucrose/10 % glycerol as described in the Materials section.

steps.title: Prepare immunostaining reagents
steps.instruction: Make Superblock™T, PBST, Tris‑EDTA buffer, M.O.M. blocking reagent, primary antibodies (HuCD 1:2000, GFAP 1:500, Sox10 1:500) and Alexa‑Fluor secondary antibodies (1:500) plus Hoechst nuclear stain (10 µg/mL). Prepare solutions immediately before use.

steps.title: Download Fiji/ImageJ
steps.instruction: Install the free Fiji/ImageJ software for later image analysis.

steps.title: Identify control tissue
steps.instruction: Select tissue of the same type as experimental samples to serve as staining controls.

steps.title: Separate muscularis propria
steps.instruction: Under a dissecting microscope, peel the muscularis propria away from the epithelium.

substeps.instruction: Add ~3 mL PBS to a silicone‑coated plate to cover tissue.
Secure tissue with pins, mucosal side up.
Zoom and focus to visualize the mucosa‑muscularis plane.
Gently grasp muscularis with curved fine forceps and mucosa with fine forceps; peel apart.
If needed, gently scrape mucosa in one area to locate the plane.
Hold muscularis down with curved forceps while peeling mucosa away.

steps.title: Label glass‑bottom plates
steps.instruction: Write tissue identifiers on the glass‑bottom well plates.

steps.title: Euthanize mouse
steps.instruction: Sacrifice the animal by CO₂ asphyxiation (or approved method).

steps.title: Expose abdominal cavity
steps.instruction: Transfer mouse to a cold dissection plate, wet abdomen with 70 % ethanol, then cut the abdominal wall laterally and vertically with scissors and forceps.

steps.title: Optional transcardial perfusion
steps.instruction: If perfusion is desired, quickly perform the following steps.

substeps.instruction: Lift sternal cartilage, secure with hemostat; cut diaphragm without damaging heart.
Cut upward toward axilla through ribs to expose anterior chest wall.
Snip right atrium with scissors.
Start pump (3–5 mL/min) and insert butterfly needle into left ventricle apex (needle pre‑primed with PBS).
Hold needle until outflow from right atrium runs clear.

steps.title: Expose intestines and lymph nodes
steps.instruction: Move intestines aside, locate mesenteric lymph nodes (string of pearls) and excise them to free bowel loops.

steps.title: Cut gastrointestinal tract
steps.instruction: Make the following cuts:

substeps.instruction: Cut at the pyloric sphincter.
Cut distal colon at the rectum.
Remove intestine from pyloric sphincter to distal colon (move gonads if needed).

steps.title: Measure intestinal segments
steps.instruction: Using a ruler, measure lengths of small intestine, colon, and cecum with minimal tension; record measurements.

steps.title: Remove mesenteric fat
steps.instruction: Gently strip mesenteric fat from the intestine with forceps or fingers.

steps.title: Segment intestine
steps.instruction: Separate the gut into defined portions for downstream applications.

substeps.instruction: Cut at ileocecal junction and at cecum‑proximal colon junction to isolate small intestine, cecum, and colon.
From the small intestine, cut a segment 10 cm proximal to the cecum.
Push intestinal contents out with the rounded edge of closed scissors.
Divide this 10 cm segment into four pieces: 1 cm segment (1 cm proximal to cecum) and three 3 cm segments (cut at 1 cm, 4 cm, and 7 cm proximal to cecum).

steps.title: Preserve 1 cm ileal segment
steps.instruction: Place the 1 cm ileal piece into an OCT‑filled mold and snap‑freeze on dry ice for possible frozen sections.

steps.title: Store larger ileal segments in RNAlater
steps.instruction: Open the 1st and 3rd 3 cm ileal pieces longitudinally, rinse in cold PBS, and place each into a microcentrifuge tube containing 600–1000 µL RNAlater (label for ileum). Do the same for the middle colon segment.

substeps.instruction: Store RNAlater tubes at –20 °C.

steps.title: Pin ileum for whole‑mount
steps.instruction: Open the 2nd 3 cm ileal segment longitudinally, rinse in cold PBS, then pin it muscle‑side down in the center of a PBS‑filled well of a silicone‑coated 6‑well plate.

substeps.instruction: Create uniform tension—just loose enough to avoid tearing but tight enough to separate cells.

steps.title: Prepare colon segments
steps.instruction: Remove colonic contents as for ileum, then:

substeps.instruction: Cut the central colon segment longitudinally, rinse in cold PBS, and place in RNAlater.
Cut the flanking 1 cm colon segments longitudinally; keep track of proximal vs distal orientation.

steps.title: Pin colon segments with ileum
steps.instruction: In the same silicone well, pin the proximal 1 cm colon segment to the left of the 3 cm ileum piece and the distal 1 cm colon segment to the right.

substeps.instruction: Maintain consistent orientation and label animal ID and date.

steps.title: Initial fixation with PFA
steps.instruction: Remove PBS from the well with a bulb suction pipette, add cold 4 % PFA in PBS (≈ 2–3 mL) to cover tissues, and handle under a chemical fume hood.

steps.title: Freeze cecum in glycerol
steps.instruction: Place the whole cecum (or as much as fits) into a 2 mL tube with 40 % glycerol in PBS, then snap‑freeze on dry ice (later store at –80 °C).

steps.title: Fix pinned tissues with Zamboni
steps.instruction: Replace PFA with Zamboni fixative, gently shake at 4 °C for 12–48 h.

steps.title: Wash and store tissues
steps.instruction: Perform the following wash sequence, then store plates at 4 °C (up to 12 months).

substeps.instruction: Remove fixative with a plastic transfer pipette.
Wash 3 × 5 min with PBS.
Add PBS + 10 % sucrose; shake at 4 °C for 2–5 h.
Remove sucrose solution.
Add PBS + 10 % glycerol + 20 % sucrose; shake at 4 °C for 12–48 h.
Remove solution, rinse once in PBS.
Add PBS + 0.1 % NaN₃, seal with parafilm, and check monthly for evaporation.

steps.title: Replace PBS with Tris‑EDTA
steps.instruction: For whole‑mount staining, discard PBS and add Tris‑EDTA buffer to each well.

steps.title: Heat‑induced epitope retrieval
steps.instruction: Incubate plates in HIER buffer at 85–95 °C for 15–60 min in a sealed lid; then cool 10–20 min.

substeps.instruction: Ensure sufficient buffer volume to prevent drying.
Optional: use bead bath or citrate buffer pH 6.0; alternatively, 30 % 1 N KOH for 30 min at RT.

steps.title: Wash after HIER
steps.instruction: Wash tissues 3 × 2 min with PBST, agitating on an orbital shaker at 18–25 °C.

steps.title: SuperblockT incubation
steps.instruction: Incubate tissues in Superblock™T for 5–10 min at 37 °C (or 30 min at 18–25 °C).

steps.title: M.O.M. blocking
steps.instruction: Prepare M.O.M. blocking solution (1 drop per 2.5 mL PBST) and add at least 500 µL per well of a 24‑well plate (1 mL for 12‑well, 2 mL for 6‑well). Incubate 5 min at 37 °C (or 15–30 min at 18–25 °C).

steps.title: Primary antibody incubation
steps.instruction: Dilute primary antibodies in Superblock™T (e.g., HuCD 1:2000, GFAP 1:500, Sox10 1:500) and incubate tissues shaking at 4 °C for 1–7 days (or 18–25 °C for 1–3 days).

steps.title: Secondary antibody incubation
steps.instruction: Wash 3 × 3–5 min with PBST, then incubate in Alexa‑Fluor secondary antibodies (1:500) at 37 °C for ~30 min (or 18–25 °C for 40–55 min).

steps.title: Nuclear staining
steps.instruction: Incubate tissues in Hoechst (10 µg/mL in PBST) for 5–10 min at 21 °C, then wash 3 × ≥ 10 min with PBST.

steps.title: Final PBS rinse
steps.instruction: Briefly rinse tissues 3 × with PBS.

steps.title: Mount tissues on glass‑bottom dishes
steps.instruction: Under a dissecting microscope, mount each tissue piece on a glass‑bottom well plate, muscle side down, keeping tissue moist.

substeps.instruction: Remove excess PBS with a pipette.
Place a drop of ProLong Gold mounting medium in the center of the well.
Gently lower a circular coverslip onto the tissue, ensuring the medium spreads and no air bubbles remain (add extra medium if needed).
Seal plate and let cure at 18–25 °C, protected from light, for 18–24 h.

steps.title: Confocal imaging
steps.instruction: Image the myenteric plexus using a confocal microscope (e.g., 20× oil immersion objective), acquiring at least three non‑overlapping fields per tissue; label files with animal ID, antibodies, and date.

steps.title: Load images into Fiji
steps.instruction: Open multichannel images in Fiji/ImageJ for analysis.

steps.title: Pre‑process images
steps.instruction: Apply Gaussian blur (sigma = 0.7) and Background Subtract (rolling ball radius = 50 px) if desired.

steps.title: Define ganglion ROI
steps.instruction: Using the freehand selection tool on GFAP channel, outline a ganglion containing ≥ 15 neuronal somata; add the ROI to the ROI Manager and save it.

steps.title: Count cells within ROI
steps.instruction: With the Cell Counter tool, manually count:

substeps.instruction: All Hoechst‑positive nuclei.
HuCD‑positive neuronal somata.
Sox10‑positive glial cells (or other markers of interest).
Save counts for each marker.

description: The protocol below describes the specific steps for assessing gastrointestinal (GI) motility in mice during, before, and after experimental manipulations, followed by tissue harvest and whole-mount immunostaining for downstream tissue analysis. Whole-gut transit testing (WGTT) is a widely used method of assessing motility in animals, including humans. We have found that there are nuances in conducting WGTT that aid in accuracy and reproducibility but that may be too specific to be outlined in a research paper methods section. Motility is affected by a vast array of factors, including time of day, anxiety level, food intake, and microbiome, so it naturally varies somewhat from day to day. However, WGTT in motility studies is often assessed at a single point in time, leading to variable results that are difficult to compare across studies and experiments. For this reason, and because it is often desirable to understand changes to GI motility longitudinally within the same individual, there is value to testing more than once per each experimental timepoint, to take an average for that time point that more accurately represents the animal’s motility. Our hope is that this protocol provides a standardized and detailed resource helpful for those conducting transit testing, particularly longitudinally. Given the essential role of the enteric nervous system (ENS) in the regulation of gastrointestinal motility, it is often of interest at the conclusion of a motility study to perform immunostaining of enteric neurons and glia. Most of the cells of the ENS are located in the myenteric plexus, which is sandwiched between the longitudinal and circular muscle layers of the intestinal wall. Because the plane containing the myenteric plexus is relatively thin (often the thickness of one neuronal cell body) and varies in tissue depth based on the thickness of surrounding tissue, it is necessary to perform whole-mount staining to see more than just a few cells of interest in a given
